subject: maths
title: Chapter 11 · Test 3
summary: Chapter 11 test 3: searching and sorting algorithms, recurrence rules, iteration and approximation — 15 questions.
body: This test covers Chapter 11 · Algorithmic thinking: linear and binary search, bubble sort and selection sort, counting comparisons, recurrence rules, the Babylonian method for square roots, fixed-point iteration, the halving method and stopping rules. Allow about 25 minutes, no notes, no calculator unless the question says. Some questions show the list or graph in a diagram — read it carefully. Work each question out on paper before you look at the options, and write your steps so you can find where you went wrong.

questions.prompt: Linear search is used to find 17 in the list shown in the diagram. How many comparisons are made, including the one that finds 17?
questions.explanation: Linear search checks from the left: 33, 5, 17 — 17 is found on comparison 3. 2 forgets to count the comparison that finds it.
steps: Linear search starts with the first item and checks each item in turn.
The items checked are 33, 5, 17, so 17 is found on comparison 3.

mistakes.B: Step 2: count the comparison with 17 itself as well — that is the one that finds it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: linear search stops as soon as it finds 17; it does not check the rest of the list.
mistakes.D: Step 1: linear search starts at the first item on the left, not at the end of the list.

questions.diagram_alt: A list of 6 boxes holding 33, 5, 17, 28, 11, 2, with positions 1 to 6 underneath.

questions.prompt: Selection sort is used on the list in the diagram (into increasing order). What is the list after the first pass?
questions.explanation: The smallest item, 2, swaps places with the first item, 7: 2, 4, 9, 7, 5. Shifting everything along is not what selection sort does.
steps: Find the smallest item in the whole list: 2.
Swap it with the first item, 7: 2, 4, 9, 7, 5.

mistakes.A: Step 2: selection sort SWAPS 2 with the first item, 7; it does not shift the other items along.
mistakes.B: Step 1: that swaps the first two neighbours, like bubble sort. Selection sort finds the smallest item first.
mistakes.D: Step 2: one pass only places one item. The rest of the list is not sorted yet.

questions.prompt: A sequence follows the rule uₙ₊₁ = 4uₙ + 1 with u₀ = 2. Find u₂.
questions.explanation: u₁ = 4 × 2 + 1 = 9 and u₂ = 4 × 9 + 1 = 37. 9 stops after one step.
steps: u₁ = 4 × 2 + 1 = 9 — substitute u₀ into the rule.
u₂ = 4 × 9 + 1 = 37 — feed u₁ back into the rule.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 9 is only u₁. Use the rule a second time to get u₂.
mistakes.C: Step 1: multiply by 4 first, then add 1 — you did them in the wrong order.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is u₃ — you used the rule one time too many.

questions.prompt: The Babylonian method improves an estimate of √60 using new x = (x + 60 ÷ x) ÷ 2. Starting with x = 10, what is the next estimate?
questions.explanation: 60 ÷ 10 = 6, and the average of 10 and 6 is 8. 16 forgets to divide by 2.
steps: Work out 60 ÷ 10 = 6.
Average with the guess: (10 + 6) ÷ 2 = 8.

mistakes.A: Step 2: after adding x and N ÷ x, divide by 2 to average them.
mistakes.B: Step 1: use N ÷ x = 60 ÷ 10 = 6, not N itself.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 6 is just N ÷ x. Average it with the guess, 10.

questions.prompt: Binary search is used to find 60 in the sorted list shown. The middle position is (low + high) ÷ 2, rounded down. Which numbers are compared with 60, in order?
questions.explanation: Halving from the middle each time compares 32, 54, 67, 60. Rounding the middle up instead gives 36, 60.
steps: Middle of 1 to 14 is position 7, which holds 32. 60 is bigger, so keep positions 8 to 14.
Middle of 8 to 14 is position 11, which holds 54. 60 is bigger, so keep positions 12 to 14.
Middle of 12 to 14 is position 13, which holds 67. 60 is smaller, so keep position 12.
Position 12 is all that is left; it holds 60 — found. So the order is 32, 54, 67, 60.

mistakes.A: Step 2: when (low + high) ÷ 2 is not a whole number, round it DOWN, not up.
mistakes.B: Step 2: after the first look, find the middle of the part that is left — do not step along one item at a time.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that is linear search. Binary search starts by looking at the middle position.

questions.diagram_alt: A sorted list of 14 boxes: 1, 4, 10, 16, 21, 25, 32, 36, 41, 49, 54, 60, 67, 72, with positions 1 to 14 underneath.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows the list 7, 5, 3, 8, 2 before bubble sort starts (sorting into increasing order). What is the list after the first pass?
questions.explanation: Walking along and swapping each out-of-order pair gives 5, 3, 7, 2, 8 — the largest value, 8, ends at the back. 3, 5, 2, 7, 8 is after two passes.
steps: Compare 7 and 5: swap → 5, 7, 3, 8, 2. Compare 7 and 3: swap → 5, 3, 7, 8, 2.
Compare 7 and 8: no swap. Compare 8 and 2: swap → 5, 3, 7, 2, 8.

mistakes.B: Step 2: one pass does not sort the whole list — it only makes sure the largest value reaches the end.
mistakes.C: Step 2: that is after the SECOND pass. Stop after one walk along the list.
mistakes.D: Step 1: keep going after the first swap — compare every neighbouring pair along the list.

questions.prompt: A sorted list has 2000 items. What is the greatest number of comparisons binary search could need?
questions.explanation: Find the smallest k with 2ᵏ ≥ 2001: 2¹⁰ = 1024 is too small and 2¹¹ = 2048 is enough, so 11.
steps: Binary search worst case: the smallest whole number k with 2ᵏ ≥ n + 1 = 2001.
2¹⁰ = 1024 is too small, but 2¹¹ = 2048 ≥ 2001, so the answer is 11.

mistakes.A: Step 1: binary search halves the list every look — 1000 is just half the list after one look.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 2000 is the worst case for linear search, not binary search.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 2¹⁰ = 1024 is less than 2001, so 10 looks are not enough. Round up, not down.

questions.prompt: A bank account follows Bₙ₊₁ = 1.03Bₙ − 100 each month (100 dollars withdrawn each month), where B₀ = $5000. Find B₂, the balance after 2 months.
questions.explanation: B₁ = 1.03 × 5000 − 100 = 5050.00 and B₂ = 1.03 × 5050.00 − 100 = 5101.50. $5100.00 wrongly earns interest on the original balance both months.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the rule multiplies by 1.03 each month — you left out the interest.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the interest in month 2 is on $5050.00, not on the original $5000.
mistakes.D: Step 1: $5050.00 is only after one month. Use the rule again for B₂.

questions.prompt: Use xₙ₊₁ = 1 + 6 ÷ xₙ with x₀ = 2 to find x₂. Give the answer to three decimal places where needed.
questions.explanation: x₁ = 1 + 6 ÷ 2 = 4 and x₂ = 1 + 6 ÷ 4 = 2.5. 2 comes from working out (1 + 6) ÷ x.
steps: x₁ = 1 + 6 ÷ 2 = 4 — divide first, then add 1.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 4 is x₁. Use the rule again to get x₂.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the rule is 1 + (6 ÷ x), not (1 + 6) ÷ x — divide before adding.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is x₃. Stop after two uses of the rule.

questions.prompt: Selection sort is used on the list 5, 8, 1, 6, 2, 7, shown in the diagram (sorting into increasing order). What is the list after the second pass?
questions.explanation: Two passes place 1 and then 2 at the front: 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 7. 1, 5, 2, 6, 7, 8 is what bubble sort gives after two passes.
steps: Pass 1: the smallest of all is 1 — swap it with the first item, 5: 1, 8, 5, 6, 2, 7.
Pass 2: the smallest of 8, 5, 6, 2, 7 is 2 — swap it with 8: 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 7.

mistakes.A: Step 2: two passes only fix the first two positions — the rest is not sorted yet.
mistakes.B: Step 1: that is after one pass. Do a second pass on the items after the first.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that is bubble sort after two passes. Selection sort moves the smallest remaining item to the front.

questions.prompt: In the worst case, how many comparisons does bubble sort make to sort 12 items (each pass stopping one place earlier than the last)?
questions.explanation: The passes make 11 + 10 + … + 1 = 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66 comparisons. 132 forgets to halve.
steps: The passes make 11, 10, …, 1 comparisons.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 12 × 12 counts every pair twice and compares items with themselves. Use n(n − 1) ÷ 2.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 12 × 11 counts every pair twice — divide by 2.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 11 is only the first pass. Add up all the passes: 11 + 10 + … + 1.

questions.prompt: Use the Babylonian method, new x = (x + 13 ÷ x) ÷ 2, with x₀ = 4 to find x₂, an estimate of √13. Give it to four decimal places.
steps: Keep x₁ unrounded: 13 ÷ 3.625 ≈ 3.586207.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 3.625 is only x₁. Use the rule a second time.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 3.5862 is just 13 ÷ x₁ — average it with x₁.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you added x₁ and N ÷ x₁ but did not divide by 2.

questions.prompt: A loan of $8000 follows Lₙ₊₁ = 1.01Lₙ − 800, where n is the number of months (1% interest per month and a $800 repayment). After how many months is the balance first below $6500?
questions.explanation: Working month by month, L₂ ≈ $6552.80 is still above $6500 but L₃ ≈ $5818.33 is below, so 3 months. Ignoring the interest gives 2.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the rule multiplies by the interest factor before taking off the repayment — without interest the balance falls too quickly.
mistakes.B: Step 2: L₀ is the starting balance, not month 1. Count from L₁.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 1% per month is ×1.01, not ×1.1. With ×1.1 the interest would cancel the repayment every month.

questions.prompt: Bubble sort is used on the list 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 to put it into increasing order. How many swaps does it make altogether?
questions.explanation: In a reversed list every pair is out of order and each pair swaps exactly once: 5 + 4 + … + 1 = 15. 5 only counts the first pass.
steps: Pass 1 moves 6 to the end with 5 swaps; pass 2 makes 4 swaps, and so on.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 5 is the swaps in the first pass only. Every later pass also swaps, one fewer each time.
mistakes.C: Step 2: every PAIR swaps once, and there are 6 × 5 ÷ 2 pairs, not 6 × 6.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 6 × 5 counts each pair twice — divide by 2.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows the iteration xₙ₊₁ = √(xₙ + 12) starting at x₀ = 0, drawn as a staircase between y = √(x + 12) and y = x. Which equation does the limiting value solve, and what is that value?

options.A: x² − x − 12 = 0, and the value is 4
options.B: x² + x − 12 = 0, and the value is 3
options.C: x² − x − 12 = 0, and the value is −3
options.D: x = √12, and the value is about 3.464

questions.explanation: At the limit x = √(x + 12), so x² − x − 12 = 0, which factorises to (x − 4)(x + 3) = 0. The iterates are square roots, so never negative: the value is 4.
steps: The limit L satisfies L = √(L + 12) — where the curve meets y = x.
Square: L² = L + 12, so L² − L − 12 = 0, which factorises to (L − 4)(L + 3) = 0.
L must be positive (it is a square root), so L = 4.

mistakes.B: Step 2: x² = x + 12 rearranges to x² − x − 12 = 0 — moving +x to the left makes it −x.
mistakes.C: Step 3: a square root is never negative, so the iterates cannot settle at −3.
mistakes.D: Step 1: √12 ≈ 3.464 is only x₁. The staircase keeps climbing past it.

questions.diagram_alt: Graph showing the curve y = square root of (x + 12), the dashed line y = x, and a green staircase starting at x0 = 0 that climbs towards where the curve meets the line.
